clue.text: " —, ironware, and cheap tin trays " (Masefield)

parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word from the cargo list in John Masefield's poem Cargoes, carried by the dirty British coaster

explanation.surface: A line of verse quoted with its first item blanked out, inviting the reader to supply it.
explanation.walkthrough: Masefield's poem Cargoes ends with a British coaster carrying 'Road-rails, pig-lead, Firewood, iron-ware, and cheap tin trays'.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank stands for one item in the poem's list of cheap cargo: logs and kindling for burning.

clue.text: High-speed trains taking off?

definitions.meaning: express trains, of the kind once called flying expresses
things that take off into the air, such as aircraft or birds

explanation.definitionFit: Express trains were nicknamed for flying along, and anything that takes off to the skies flies.

clue.text: Put the record in the holder again

definitions.text: Put the record in the holder again

indicators.note: the word for the record is set inside the word for the holder

parts.note: a rack is a holder or stand
EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: Someone puts a disc back in its stand after playing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts EP inside RACK; the whole clue also describes stowing things away a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: To pack again is to return something to its container a second time, which is what the clue describes.

clue.text: Support for joists, or a decorative dish?

definitions.meaning: a timber laid along the top of a wall on which joists or rafters rest
a china plate made to hang on a wall as ornament

explanation.definitionFit: In building, a horizontal timber on a wall carries the joists; read literally, the phrase is an ornamental plate hung up for display.

clue.text: Only this dual formation is in a queer style

indicators.note: a formation is an arrangement, so these letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a pairing of two things is oddly arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'formation' rearranges ONLY THIS DUAL, twelve letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: Queer here has its old sense of strange, and something done bizarrely is done in an odd or eccentric way.

clue.text: Least lively part I can play

definitions.text: Least lively part I can play

parts.words: Least lively part I can play
parts.note: a role in which one does nothing at all, as an animal does when it feigns death to escape a predator

explanation.surface: An actor jokes about the dullest role they could be cast in.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'play possum' is to pretend to be dead, as the American opossum does when threatened.
explanation.definitionFit: The marsupial is famous for shamming death, so the part it plays is the least animated imaginable.

clue.text: De Quincey's self-confessed diet

parts.note: Thomas De Quincey wrote Confessions of an English ... -Eater, admitting his addiction to a drug

explanation.surface: A note on what a famous essayist admitted to eating.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer's memoir confessed to his habit of taking the poppy-derived narcotic, his 'diet' in a joking sense.

clue.text: The State has uncommonly long ears

indicators.note: uncommonly means in an unusual way, so these letters are arranged unusually

explanation.surface: A remark that a country's people have unusually long ears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' rearranges LONG EARS; the answer is a state of Malaysia.
explanation.definitionFit: Selangor is one of the states of the Malaysian federation, on the west coast of the peninsula.

clue.text: Who'd need us, say, to make a living?

definitions.text: Who'd need us, say, to make a living?

parts.words: Who'd need us, say, to make a living?
parts.note: 'need' with 'say' suggests its sound-alike knead, the working motion of those who rub muscles for pay

explanation.surface: Someone wonders which people depend on others like them for their income.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' tells you to hear 'need' as 'knead': these workers knead their clients to earn their keep.
explanation.definitionFit: Professionals who give body rubs work the flesh with their hands, kneading customers for a fee.

clue.text: I am North European, holding Italian to be rude

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm

indicators.note: holding means the European is wrapped around the Italian

parts.note: a Pole is a native of Poland, in northern Europe
IT is a common abbreviation for Italian, as in vermouth

explanation.surface: Someone from northern Europe confesses to thinking an Italian ill-mannered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts IT inside POLE, after IM.
explanation.definitionFit: Being discourteous and being ill-mannered are the same thing: a synonym pair.

clue.text: Cesario's flowers, by another name

parts.note: Cesario is the name the heroine of Shakespeare's Twelfth Night takes in disguise; her real name is also a garden plant

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what blooms belong to a Shakespearean page, if called something else.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night the shipwrecked heroine disguises herself as the youth Cesario; her own name is also a flower related to the pansy.
explanation.definitionFit: The plants are pansy relatives sharing the name of the heroine who calls herself Cesario.

clue.text: Prometheus Bound one of these suspense stories

definitions.meaning: in Greek myth Prometheus was chained to a rocky crag, left dangling on a precipice
serials that end each episode on an unresolved moment of tension

explanation.definitionFit: Tales ending on a tense, unresolved moment take their name from someone dangling from a precipice, as the chained Titan literally did.

clue.text: Go over it again with a backward horse

indicators.note: backward means the word for the horse is read from end to start

parts.note: a pacer is a horse trained to a lateral gait, used in harness racing

explanation.surface: A rider takes a reluctant horse round the course once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns PACER round.
explanation.definitionFit: To summarise again is to go back over the main points: a synonym for reviewing.

clue.text: Made Allen change the dance

indicators.note: change means alter, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone forced a man named Allen to switch to a different dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges MADE ALLEN.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a stately court dance of German origin, a movement in many Baroque suites.

clue.text: Miss Cheesecake — attendant of Miss Bright?

definitions.meaning: a small almond or curd tart, a Richmond speciality, which bears a lady's title
an unmarried bridesmaid who leads the others at a wedding, 'bright' hinting at the radiant bride

explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a curd tart from Richmond and to the chief bridesmaid who attends a radiant young bride.

clue.text: More a film version of an historic banner

indicators.note: a version is a rendering, so these letters are given a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A remake of a film about a famous old flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of' rearranges MORE A FILM.
explanation.definitionFit: The oriflamme was the red-gold standard of the early French kings, carried into battle.

clue.text: Being about three quarters of port's 22

indicators.note: about means the word placed around the compass letters

parts.note: three of the four compass points, E S W

explanation.surface: A measure of a bottle of port and its sediment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts ESW, three of the four cardinal points, inside BEING; 22 refers to 22-down, the deposit in old port.
explanation.definitionFit: Beeswing is the filmy deposit that forms in long-kept port, a type of the sediment named at 22.

clue.text: Beer for Mum — water for him

definitions.text: Beer for Mum — water for him

parts.words: Beer for Mum — water for him
parts.note: Mum is an old strong beer; for the first man in Eden, his only drink was the plain liquid from springs

explanation.surface: A family drinks order: beer for mother, water for father.
explanation.walkthrough: Mum was a kind of strong ale; the answer is a jocular name for water, the only 'beer' the first man had.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain water is jokingly named after the first man in Eden, who had nothing else to drink.

clue.text: Non-stop smoker's conveyor?

parts.note: one who smokes one after another is a chain smoker; a belt running round without a break carries goods

explanation.surface: A joke about the supply line that keeps a heavy smoker going.
explanation.walkthrough: A chain smoker lights one cigarette from the last; the answer is also an engineering term for a looped conveyor.
explanation.definitionFit: A loop of linked parts with no break runs continuously, as in a conveyor or bucket elevator.

clue.text: It's the devil's at one's fingertips

definitions.text: It's the devil's at one's fingertips

parts.words: It's the devil's at one's fingertips
parts.note: the devil's version of a drumming display is the idle, impatient tapping of fingers on a table

explanation.surface: Something devilish is said to be close at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'devil's tattoo' is an idle drumming with the fingers, from tattoo meaning a drumbeat.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhythmic drumbeat on fingers, the devil's sort, is impatient tapping on a surface.

clue.text: The Gilpins had been for 20 years with no holiday

definitions.text: The Gilpins had been for 20 years with no holiday

parts.words: The Gilpins had been for 20 years with no holiday
parts.note: in Cowper's John Gilpin, Mrs Gilpin tells her husband they have been married twice ten tedious years without a day off

explanation.surface: A married couple has gone two decades without a break.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowper's ballad has Mrs Gilpin say 'though wedded we have been these twice ten tedious years, yet we no holiday have seen'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gilpins were married, joined as husband and wife, for those twenty years.

clue.text: Stop one's monocle getting broken'

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, so these letters are put back together differently

parts.note: one is I, and the 's adds S

explanation.surface: Someone's eyeglass is about to snap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting broken' rearranges I, S and MONOCLE; 'Stop' means a punctuation mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A punctuation mark is called a stop, and this one marks a pause longer than a comma.

clue.text: Beggar's fare for the vineyard saint

parts.note: cru is French for a vineyard or its wine growth

explanation.surface: A vagrant's meal is offered to the patron saint of vineyards.
explanation.walkthrough: CRU, French for a wine-growing estate, then ST for saint.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry heel of bread is the proverbial food of the poor beggar.

clue.text: Taken by a departing guest

parts.note: a visitor going home is said to 'take' this, meaning to say goodbye

explanation.surface: Something a guest takes on the way out, as if pocketing a souvenir.
explanation.walkthrough: One 'takes one's leave' on departing; the clue makes it sound like something stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: Permission to go, or a farewell, is what one 'takes' when departing.

clue.text: One of the early 1 dn who came unstuck

definitions.text: One of the early 1 dn who came unstuck

parts.words: One of the early 1 dn who came unstuck
parts.note: an early airman of Greek myth whose wings, fixed with wax, fell apart near the sun

explanation.surface: A pioneer aviator whose career ended badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 dn is the airborne travellers at 1-down; this one's waxed wings literally came unstuck when he flew too near the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth Daedalus's son flew on wings of feather and wax which melted, so he fell into the sea.

clue.text: He and Edward go round the tree in top gear

indicators.note: go round means the letters of the first word sit on either side of the tree

parts.note: taken as written
the elm is a tree
Ted is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Two people drive round a tree as fast as they can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go round' puts ELM inside HE, then TED follows. 'Top gear' is not driving speed but headwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing protective headwear means having gear on top of one's head.

clue.text: Sound places for 1 ac in an Oxford exam

indicators.note: sound tells you to hear the words said aloud rather than spelt

parts.note: fireplace grates are where logs, the answer to 1-across, burn

explanation.surface: Someone seeks good places to put fuel in an Oxford examination room.
explanation.walkthrough: GRATES, where 1-across burns, sounds like the answer, the Oxford final exam in classics (Literae Humaniores).
explanation.definitionFit: The final honours examination in classics at Oxford University has this informal name.

clue.text: A compound heavenly body

parts.note: a steroid is an organic chemical compound

explanation.surface: A celestial object described as being made of mixed materials.
explanation.walkthrough: A then STEROID.
explanation.definitionFit: A minor planet orbiting the sun is one of the bodies of the sky.
